title: Broadband Polarization Compensation with Link Segment Reconstruction for Quantum Optical Links
authors: Qingyu Shi, Erwan Trad, Julien Chénedé, Tobias Vogl
abstract: Polarization-encoded quantum communication requires compensation of polarization transformations induced by the optical links. If the compensator is embedded between two channel segments, the transformations before and after the compensator must be treated separately. Moreover, standard three-wave-plate polarization controllers can become non-universal when their retardances deviate from their ideal values. To address these two challenges, we introduce a four-wave plate compensator that synthesizes arbitrary SO(3) polarization transformations over a broad wavelength range, and an eight-Stokes vector protocol that reconstructs the two link-segment Mueller matrices on either side of the compensator. Our experiment reveals that the four-plate sequence suppresses polarization-induced excess quantum bit error rate (QBER) to the sub-percent level at an operating wavelength more than 100 nm from the design wavelength without further optimization. Combined with two auxiliary wavelengths, our scheme tracks the temperature-driven drift of a strongly wavelength-sensitive fiber spool while keeping the excess QBER below 1%. These results support flexible compensator placement and wavelength channel selection, as well as non-interruptive polarization control in wavelength-division-multiplexed quantum optical links.
summary: The paper presents a robust method for compensating polarization transformations in quantum optical links using a novel four-wave plate compensator. By combining this hardware with an eight-Stokes vector protocol, the authors achieve sub-percent QBER suppression over wide bandwidths and successfully track temperature-induced drift via auxiliary wavelength measurements.
main_problem: Polarization-encoded quantum communication requires compensating for polarization transformations induced by optical links, which is complicated by embedded compensators and non-ideal waveplate retardances.
main_result: The developed four-wave plate sequence suppresses polarization-induced excess QBER to the sub-percent level across broad wavelengths, and auxiliary wavelength feedback maintains low error rates during temperature drift.
method: The authors introduce a novel four-plate compensator and an eight-Stokes vector protocol to reconstruct link segment Mueller matrices ($	ext{M}_\alpha, 	ext{M}_ eta$) surrounding the compensator.
model_or_system: The system models quantum optical links using polarization encoding, where transformations are described by $	ext{SO}(3)$ Mueller matrices. The experiment uses fiber spools as Device Under Test (DUTs) to simulate real-world link impairments.
key_observables: Excess Quantum Bit Error Rate ($	ext{QBER}_{	ext{pol}}$), reconstructed link segment Mueller matrices, and axis-angle parameters $(	ilde{\epsilon}, 	ilde{\alpha}, 	ilde{ eta}, 	ilde{\gamma})$.
important_parameters: Wavelength range ($>100 	ext{ nm}$ bandwidth), temperature variation ($\Delta T$), and the required condition for retardance error suppression.
main_assumptions: Polarization-dependent loss and depolarization are not treated as compensable errors; reconstruction relies on measuring known input states at specific waveplate settings.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the experimental setup, long-term monitoring of polarization drift over temperature using auxiliary wavelengths, and comparisons between different compensation sequences (Q-Q-Q-H vs. Q-Q-H).
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the need for robust compensation in embedded links. It then details the four-plate compensator synthesis and the eight-Stokes vector reconstruction protocol. Finally, it demonstrates performance by testing broadband operation and long-term stability against temperature drift using auxiliary wavelengths.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses practical challenges in quantum networking hardware—namely, maintaining polarization fidelity across varying environmental conditions (temperature) and spectral bandwidths—which is crucial for deploying quantum communication infrastructure.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Experimental setup. In the present implementation, the optical switch selects one fiber-coupled laser at a time. The input state is prepared by a QWP followed by a linear polarizer on a motorized rotation mount. The transforma- tions before the compensator, through the compensator, and after the compensator are denoted by Mα, M, and Mβ, re- spectively. The compensator is a motorized stack of three QWPs followed by one HWP in the propagation direction. DUT: device under test. The output Stokes vectors are mea- sured with a polarimeter.

Fig. 1 shows the experimental implementation used for the two-step reconstruction and compensation procedure. The motorized Q-Q-Q-H compensator is placed between the input-side transformation Mα and the output-side transformation Mβ. For each fixed wavelength, the com- pensation setting was obtained in two steps. First, we reconstructed Mα and Mβ using the eight-Stokes vector measurement protocol. Second, we calculated the Q-Q- Q-H wave plate angles required to implement the com- pensating matrix in Eq. (3).
